title: Gases in the atmosphere
learningObjective: Know the approximate percentages by volume of the four most abundant gases in dry air; Understand how to determine the percentage by volume of oxygen in air using experiments involving the reactions of metals (e.g. iron) and non-metals (e.g. phosphorus) with air; Describe the combustion of elements in oxygen, including magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur; Describe the formation of carbon dioxide from the thermal decomposition of metal carbonates, including copper(II) carbonate; Know that carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas and that increasing amounts in the atmosphere may contribute to climate change; Practical: Determine the approximate percentage by volume of oxygen in air using a metal or a non-metal

sections.title: Gases in the Atmosphere
sections.markdown:
The atmosphere is the blanket of gas held around the Earth by gravity, and
you are breathing a sample of it right now. That sample is a **mixture**:
several different gases jumbled together, each keeping its own properties,
none of them chemically joined to the others. This chapter takes that
mixture apart. You will learn exactly what dry air is made of and in what
proportions, then meet the experiments that measure one particular
component — oxygen — directly, and finally follow the two gases that
matter most for chemical reactions and for the climate: **oxygen** and
**carbon dioxide**.

The chapter runs on one measuring idea, stated here so everything
afterwards has a home: a gas's share of a mixture is quoted as a
**[[percentage-by-volume]]** — of every 100 cm³ of [[dry-air]], about
78 cm³ is nitrogen and about 21 cm³ is oxygen. Three different
experiments (heated copper, rusting iron, burning phosphorus) all attack
the same question from different angles: remove the oxygen from a known
volume of air, watch the volume shrink, and do one subtraction and one
division. Whichever reagent you use, the arithmetic and the error
analysis are the same shape — and that shape is where the exam marks
live.

From measurement the chapter moves to reaction. **[[combustion]]** —
burning elements in oxygen — produces a family of compounds called
**oxides**, and comparing the oxides of metals with the oxides of
non-metals reveals a clean, examinable split in their properties. The
same chemistry explains where atmospheric carbon dioxide comes from, and
why that particular gas, despite being only about 0.04% of the air,
punches far above its concentration: it is a **[[greenhouse-gas]]**, and
the final sections of this chapter make you explain — at the level of
molecular vibrations — why carbon dioxide absorbs infrared radiation
while nitrogen and oxygen, 99% of the air between them, do not.

Every objective in this chapter is **core content: it can be examined in
both Paper 1C and Paper 2C**. By the end you will be able to recall the
composition of dry air; describe and calculate the oxygen-percentage
experiments using metals or non-metals (the listed practical); describe
the combustion of magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur in oxygen, with
equations; describe carbon dioxide forming from heated metal carbonates,
including copper(II) carbonate; and explain the greenhouse effect in
infrared terms.

:::prior-knowledge
Three earlier chapters load this one. From Chapter 1 (u1:c01) you need
the particle model — gases fill their container, particles are far apart,
and a gas sample's volume is really the volume of its container. From
Chapter 5 (u1:c05) you need word and balanced equations with state
symbols, because every reaction in this chapter is written out in full.
From Chapters 7 and 8 (u1:c07, u1:c08) you need the ionic/covalent split:
metal oxides are ionic compounds, non-metal oxides are covalent molecules,
and that distinction drives the property split later in the chapter.
Chapter 14 (u2:c14) develops rusting properly — here you *use* rusting
as a measuring tool — and Chapter 18 (u2:c18) owns the gas tests,
including the hydrogen "squeaky pop" this chapter mentions.
:::

:::exam-hint
Nothing in this chapter is chemistry-only, so every fact and every
explanation here can appear on Paper 1C as well as Paper 2C. The
oxygen-percentage practical is one of the most reliably examined
practicals in the whole specification: expect both a
*describe-the-method* question and a *calculate-the-percentage* question,
and expect a follow-up demanding the error analysis ("give one reason the
answer came out too low"). The composition figures themselves are pure
recall — four numbers that cost nothing to learn and pay every year.
:::

:::misconception
"Air is mostly oxygen — that's what we breathe." Breathing *feels* like
the reason air exists, but it is not the reason air is mostly what it
is. Nitrogen makes up about four-fifths of the air and oxygen only about
one-fifth; every breath takes in far more nitrogen than oxygen. Students
who guess "oxygen" on the composition question hand the mark away — the
examiner is testing whether you learned the table or trusted your gut.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.9 recall items. Before moving on, say the four
most abundant gases in dry air and their approximate percentages from
memory. If you can do that without looking, this chapter's foundation is
already in place — the rest of the chapter builds measurement and
explanation on top of those four numbers.
:::

sections.title: The Composition of the Air
sections.markdown:
Learn the composition of unpolluted, [[dry-air]] as a table first and a
story second. The four most abundant gases, quoted as approximate
**[[percentage-by-volume]]** figures:

| Gas | Amount in air (%) | Amount in air (fraction) |
|---|---|---|
| nitrogen | 78.1 | about 4/5 |
| oxygen | 21.0 | about 1/5 |
| argon | 0.9 | — |
| carbon dioxide | 0.04 | — |

Nitrogen and oxygen between them account for about 99% of the air, with
argon — one of the noble gases — making up most of the remainder. The
other noble gases (helium, neon, krypton, xenon) are present too, but in
amounts so small they round to nothing at this level of precision. Read
the fraction column as the examiner's shorthand: "about one-fifth oxygen"
is the sentence the mark scheme rewards, and it is the sentence the
experiments in this section are designed to confirm.

:::key-point
These figures apply **only to dry, unpolluted air**. Ordinary air can
carry anywhere between 0 and 4% water vapour on top of everything in the
table, which is why the table is always stated for dry air. And although
carbon dioxide's percentage is tiny, it is **rising steadily** because of
human activity — a fact this chapter returns to in the greenhouse
sections.
:::

One measurement dominates this chapter: the percentage of oxygen. The
strategy is always the same — react something with the oxygen in a known
volume of air and watch how much the volume decreases as the oxygen is
removed. The first method uses copper metal, and it is worth mastering
the apparatus carefully because every other method in this chapter is a
variation on its logic.

The apparatus is a pair of **[[gas-syringe]]**s joined through a silica
tube packed with copper turnings. The procedure:

- Push one plunger fully in and set the other at 100 cm³. The system now
  contains exactly 100 cm³ of air.
- Heat the silica tube strongly with a roaring Bunsen flame.
- Push the left plunger in: air is forced over the heated copper and the
  right plunger moves out to receive it.
- Push the plungers in sequence, back and forth, so the air keeps
  passing over the hot copper. The pink-brown copper turns black as
  copper(II) oxide forms on it.
- As the copper reacts, slide the Bunsen burner along the tube so the
  flame is always heating fresh copper.
- Watch the total gas volume fall as oxygen is consumed. Keep sweeping
  the air until the volume **no longer changes**.
- Let the apparatus cool back to room temperature, then take the final
  reading — gases expand when heated, so a hot reading would be too high.

:::safety
Wear eye protection and heat carefully: a flame applied clumsily can
crack the glass syringe. Take care not to push the opposite plunger
completely out of its barrel during the sweeping.
:::

A typical result set:

| Measurement | Volume |
|---|---|
| initial volume of air in the system / cm³ | 100 |
| final volume of 'air' in the system / cm³ | 79 |

The volume fell by 21 cm³, and the next section converts that fall into
the percentage of oxygen. Two facts make the method work, and both are
examinable in their own right.

:::key-point
The copper must be **in [[excess]]** — more than enough to react with
all the oxygen in the air sample. You will see unreacted copper left at
the end, and that is deliberate: if the copper ran out first, some
oxygen would survive unreacted and the percentage you calculate would be
**too low**.
:::

:::key-point
The final 79 cm³ is called 'air' in inverted commas because it is no
longer really air — the oxygen has gone and what remains is mostly
nitrogen. Nitrogen is very unreactive: put a lighted splint into this
leftover gas and the splint goes out, because **oxygen is needed for
things to burn**. That observation is itself evidence the experiment did
its job.
:::

:::exam-hint
"State why the apparatus is allowed to cool before the final volume is
recorded" is a one-mark gift if you know the particle model: gases
expand when heated, so a reading taken hot overstates the final volume
and understates the calculated oxygen percentage. And in
describe-the-method questions, the phrase the mark scheme wants for the
end-point is **"until there is no further change in volume"** — not
"until it looks finished".
:::

:::misconception
"The volume goes down because the copper takes up space / the copper is
lost." The volume falls because **oxygen gas is removed from the gas
mixture** — it reacts with the copper and becomes part of a solid
(copper(II) oxide) sitting on the tube's surface. Solids contribute
essentially nothing to the gas volume. The copper itself is in excess:
whatever volume change you measure belongs to the oxygen, which is
exactly why the method measures oxygen.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.9/2.10 items on composition and the copper
method. Test yourself: what fraction of dry air is oxygen? Why must the
copper be in excess? What colour change does the copper show, and what
compound is the black product? Why cool the apparatus before the final
reading? Four right answers and the copper method is yours.
:::

sections.title: Results
sections.markdown:
Every oxygen-percentage experiment ends the same way: the volume drop is
the volume of oxygen that reacted, and one division turns that into a
percentage. For the copper experiment, the volume fell from 100 cm³ to
79 cm³ because the oxygen was removed as it reacted:

2Cu(s) + O₂(g) → 2CuO(s)

copper + oxygen → copper(II) oxide

The volume of oxygen that reacted was 100 − 79 = **21 cm³**. The
original air sample was 100 cm³, so:

percentage of oxygen = 21/100 × 100 = **21%**

That is the whole calculation — subtraction, then a percentage. The
iron-rusting version of the experiment asks exactly the same question,
but the arithmetic has one extra step because the apparatus holds air in
three separate places, and the examiner expects you to handle all three.

:::worked-example
**Worked example: the percentage of oxygen in air from the rusting of
iron.** Wet iron filings sit in a conical flask joined to a gas syringe;
the air's volume is measured in three parts. Use this data:

| Measurement | Volume |
|---|---|
| volume of air in conical flask / cm³ | 130 |
| volume of air in connecting tube / cm³ | 12 |
| initial reading on gas syringe / cm³ | 92 |
| final reading on gas syringe / cm³ | 43 |

**Step 1 — total volume of air at the start.** Add all three volumes:
130 + 12 + 92 = **234 cm³**.

**Step 2 — total volume of 'air' at the end.** The oxygen is gone but
the leftover gas still fills flask, tube and syringe: 130 + 12 + 43 =
**185 cm³**.

**Step 3 — volume of oxygen used up.** 234 − 185 = **49 cm³**.

**Step 4 — percentage of oxygen.** 49/234 × 100 = 20.9 ≈ **21%**.

The three-volume bookkeeping is the part students drop marks on: the
oxygen was spread through flask, tube *and* syringe, so the percentage
is 49 out of 234, never 49 out of 92.
:::

The **[[rusting]]** of iron is the slow chemistry doing the same job —
iron rusts in damp air, using up oxygen as it does so, and that reaction
is the measuring tool:

- Put wet iron filings in a conical flask connected to a gas syringe.
- Before starting, measure the volume of air inside the apparatus:
  fill the flask and connecting tube with water, then transfer the
  water to a measuring cylinder. (The small volume occupied by the iron
  filings itself is negligible.)
- Record the initial gas-syringe reading.
- Leave the apparatus for about a **week**, until the reading stops
  changing — rusting is slow.
- Record the final reading, then run the four-step calculation above.

:::key-point
Iron needs **both oxygen and water** to rust — dry iron in dry air does
not rust, and iron underwater with no dissolved oxygen does not either.
That is why the filings are *wet*: the water lets the rusting reaction
proceed, and the reaction consumes the oxygen. Rusting is treated fully
as a corrosion problem in Chapter 14 (u2:c14); here it is your oxygen
removal mechanism.
:::

:::safety
Iron filings can irritate the skin and are a particular hazard if they
get into the eyes — handle them with a spatula, not fingers, and wear
eye protection.
:::

Sometimes the iron experiment comes out **below 21%**. Two standard
reasons, and the mark scheme wants them in this form:

- **Not left long enough** — the iron has not had the chance to react
  with all the oxygen in the apparatus, so some oxygen survives and the
  measured drop is too small.
- **Not enough iron at the start** — the iron must be in [[excess]],
  enough to react with every trace of oxygen; if the iron runs out
  first, the leftover oxygen never gets counted.

Notice both errors push the answer the same way — down. A well-run
experiment with excess iron and enough time converges on 21% from
either direction.

The third method is a demonstration rather than a class experiment,
because it uses white phosphorus, but it is the fastest of the three.
Phosphorus is so reactive that it burns in the oxygen of ordinary air,
forming a phosphorus oxide that dissolves readily in water — and the
water's job in the apparatus matters twice over.

- Set up a bell jar standing in water, with a small evaporating basin
  floating on the water carrying a piece of phosphorus.
- Mark the initial water level on the outside of the jar.
- Remove the bung, touch the phosphorus with a hot metal wire to ignite
  it, and replace the bung quickly.
- The phosphorus burns inside the jar, filling it with white smoke; the
  water level **rises** as oxygen is consumed. The smoke then clears as
  the oxide dissolves in the water.
- When the water level stops rising, mark the final level.
- Measure the change by turning the jar upside down, filling it with
  water to each mark in turn, and pouring into a large measuring
  cylinder.

:::key-point
Phosphorus does not react with water — that is what lets it sit on a
floating basin inside a jar whose lower half is underwater. It reacts
with the *oxygen* above the waterline instead, which is precisely the
gas you are measuring.
:::

:::safety
This is a teacher demonstration. The demonstrator wears goggles or a
face shield and works in a well-ventilated room. The bell jar must be
held down firmly at the start, because the pressure rises as burning
begins. And once the fumes have cleared, the evaporating basin is
sunk with a glass rod — unreacted phosphorus left in warm, damp air can
re-ignite.
:::

The experiments above share one idea with everything that follows:
oxygen is reactive, and its reactions with elements are worth naming.
Elements that burn in oxygen take part in **[[combustion]]** reactions,
and an element burns more brightly and more rapidly in pure oxygen than
in air — because air is only 21% oxygen, while a jar of pure oxygen is
100% of it. Sulfur, one of the elements you will burn in the next
section, gives a product with a name pair worth fixing now.

:::key-point
Sulfur dioxide is also called **sulfur(IV) oxide**. And when it
dissolves in water the product is **[[sulfurous-acid]]** (H₂SO₃) —
**not** sulfuric acid (H₂SO₄). The "-ous" acid carries the "- dioxide"
gas; keep the pair matched and the naming marks are safe.
:::

:::exam-hint
All three methods get asked as "why must the [copper / iron /
phosphorus] be in excess?" and the answer is always the same sentence
with the reagent swapped in: **so that all the oxygen in the sample
reacts** — otherwise some oxygen survives and the calculated percentage
is too low. Learn that sentence once and it answers three experiments.
Also expect the reverse question: "give one reason the student's answer
was below 21%" — the two iron-method reasons (insufficient time,
insufficient iron) are the mark-scheme bank.
:::

:::misconception
"A result below 21% means the air that day really contained less
oxygen." The composition of the atmosphere does not drift by several
percent between lessons — a low result is an **experimental error**, not
an atmospheric fact. Trace the error to its mechanism: unreacted oxygen
left behind (too little time or too little iron), or volume readings
taken at the wrong temperature. Examiners reward answers that name the
mechanism, not answers that shrug at the number.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.10/2.14 items on the oxygen-percentage
practicals plus spec 2.11 combustion recall. Run the copper numbers
without notes (100 → 79 gives what percentage?). Then explain why wet
iron filings rather than dry ones, and why the phosphorus basin floats
on water. Finally: what acid forms when sulfur dioxide dissolves in
water — and what is it *not* called?
:::

sections.title: Metal Oxides
sections.markdown:
When an element burns in oxygen the product is an **[[oxide]]**, and
each element announces its combustion with a characteristic flame and a
characteristic product. Three elements are named by the specification —
magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur — and you should be able to give the
observation, the equation and the product for each.

**Magnesium** burns in oxygen with an **extremely bright white flame**,
leaving a white, powdery ash of magnesium oxide:

2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s)

The white powder is not very soluble in water, but a very small amount
does dissolve, and the tiny quantity that does reacts to give an
**alkaline** solution of magnesium hydroxide:

MgO(s) + H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂(aq)

That slant — metal oxide meeting water and coming out alkaline — is the
first hint of the metal/non-metal oxide split, which the next section
turns into a full set of rules.

**Sulfur** burns in oxygen with a **blue flame**, producing a
poisonous, **colourless** gas, sulfur dioxide:

S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)

The gas dissolves in water to form an acidic solution of sulfurous
acid:

SO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → H₂SO₃(aq)

(Section 3's key point is worth repeating in equation form: the acid
here is sulfurous acid, H₂SO₃ — sulfuric acid, H₂SO₄, is a different
substance with two more oxygens.)

**Hydrogen** burns in oxygen with a **pale blue flame**, and the only
product is water:

2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)

Hydrogen's combustion has a second face: ignite a *mixture* of hydrogen
and oxygen — rather than burning hydrogen in a jar of oxygen — and it
explodes with a characteristic squeaky pop. That explosion is the basis
of the standard laboratory test for hydrogen gas, which lives in
Chapter 18 (u2:c18) with the rest of the gas tests.

:::exam-hint
Combustion questions are observation-plus-equation questions, and the
marks split between them. The observation bank to memorise: magnesium —
*extremely bright white flame, white powder*; sulfur — *blue flame,
poisonous colourless gas*; hydrogen — *pale blue flame, water formed*.
Note the deliberate contrast: sulfur's **flame** is blue and hydrogen's
**flame** is pale blue, but sulfur's product is a colourless gas while
hydrogen's product is a colourless liquid. Writing "yellow" or "green"
for sulfur dioxide is a lost mark — the yellow you may be picturing is
the sulfur element itself.
:::

:::misconception
"Burning is the same as heating — both need a flame." A flame is the
*sign* of combustion, not its cause. **Combustion** is a chemical
reaction: the element combining with oxygen, with energy released.
Heating magnesium gently in air *without* ignition does nothing; ignite
it, and the magnesium atoms react with oxygen molecules to build magnesium
oxide. In equations, the oxygen is a **reactant** — if O₂ is not on the
left-hand side, the reaction is not combustion.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.11 items on combustion of elements in oxygen.
Cover the equations and reconstruct them from the elements' names; then
cover the observations and recite the three flame colours and products.
Finish by writing the balanced equation for each combustion with state
symbols — the full six-mark skeleton for this spec point.
:::

sections.title: The Properties of Oxides
sections.markdown:
Magnesium oxide dissolving to give an alkaline solution and sulfur
dioxide dissolving to give an acidic one are not accidents — they are
two halves of a pattern that runs through the whole of chemistry. When
elements burn in oxygen, you can generalise about the **[[oxide]]**s
they form, and the generalisation follows the metal/non-metal line you
already know from the Periodic Table (u1:c04).

**Metal oxides** are ionic compounds, built from metal ions and oxide
ions (O²⁻):

- they are usually **basic oxides**, which means they react with acids
  to form salts;
- they are usually **insoluble** in water;
- the ones that *are* soluble react with the water to form **alkaline**
  solutions containing hydroxide (OH⁻) ions — magnesium hydroxide from
  magnesium oxide is the worked case from the previous section.

**Non-metal oxides** are covalent molecular compounds:

- they are usually **acidic oxides**, which react with alkalis and bases
  to form salts;
- they are **often soluble** in water, reacting with it to form
  **acidic** solutions containing hydrogen (H⁺) ions — sulfur dioxide's
  sulfurous acid is the example already on your page, and carbon
  dioxide behaves the same way.

Learn the two lists as mirror images: ionic vs covalent, basic vs
acidic, insoluble vs often soluble, alkaline vs acidic solutions. One
element, one side of the divide — that is the entire rule set.

Carbon dioxide deserves its own introduction, because the next two
sections follow it into the atmosphere. It is a colourless gas, most
easily made in the laboratory by reacting dilute hydrochloric acid with
calcium carbonate in the form of marble chips:

CaCO₃(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + CO₂(g) + H₂O(l)

But there is a second route to carbon dioxide that matters for this
chapter: heat most metal **carbonates** strongly and they split apart,
giving the metal oxide and carbon dioxide. Breaking a compound up by
heating it is called **[[thermal-decomposition]]**:

- copper(II) carbonate is a **green** powder that decomposes on heating
  to give **black** copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide:

  CuCO₃(s) → CuO(s) + CO₂(g)

- calcium carbonate needs a much higher temperature before it
  decomposes — and the reaction is commercially important, because it
  converts limestone (calcium carbonate) into quicklime (calcium
  oxide):

  CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

:::exam-hint
Fix the two colours now and keep them for the rest of the course:
copper(II) **carbonate is green**, copper(II) **oxide is black**. The
green-to-black colour change on heating is the observation question for
copper(II) carbonate's thermal decomposition, and it also fingerprints
the black coating formed in the copper-oxygen experiment back in
Section 2 — same black compound, copper(II) oxide, made two different
ways.
:::

:::misconception
"Heating copper(II) carbonate is combustion — both need a Bunsen
burner." The Bunsen burner supplies heat in both cases, but the
chemistry is different. **Combustion** is an element or compound
*reacting with oxygen* — oxygen is a reactant and appears on the left of
the equation. **Thermal decomposition** is *one compound splitting
into two or more products* using heat alone — no oxygen is consumed, and
CO₂ appears on the right as a *product*. If oxygen were a reactant,
copper(II) carbonate could not decompose in a sealed jar; it can, and
that is the test of the distinction.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.12 items on carbonate decomposition plus spec
2.11 combustion links. Say the two generalisation lists (metal vs
non-metal oxides) from memory; write the equation for copper(II)
carbonate decomposing; state the colours before and after; and write
the laboratory equation for making carbon dioxide from marble chips and
hydrochloric acid.
:::

sections.title: Carbon Dioxide and Global Warming: the Greenhouse Effect
sections.markdown:
Carbon dioxide enters the atmosphere whenever fossil fuels burn — and
fossil fuels burn everywhere in a modern economy. Coal is mostly carbon,
and burning it in excess oxygen is the simplest combustion there is:

C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g)

Petrol is a mixture containing many different **[[hydrocarbon]]**s
(compounds of carbon and hydrogen only — they are treated fully in
Unit 4, starting at Chapter 22 (u4:c22)). One typical component, octane
(C₈H₁₈), burns to give carbon dioxide and water in a ratio worth
checking yourself: the equation is balanced atom for atom.

2C₈H₁₈(l) + 25O₂(g) → 16CO₂(g) + 18H₂O(l)

Every hydrocarbon molecule that burns adds its carbon to the atmosphere
as carbon dioxide, and for roughly the last 200 years — since the
industrial revolution — the level of CO₂ in the atmosphere has been
**increasing**, driven by the burning of fossil fuels and by
deforestation (cutting down trees for agriculture, which removes the
plants that absorb CO₂).

Why should a gas present at only 0.04% of the atmosphere carry so much
weight? Because carbon dioxide is a **[[greenhouse-gas]]** — one of a
select group of gases that interact with the radiation the Earth sends
back out into space. The mechanism runs in four steps:

1. High-energy **ultraviolet and visible light** from the Sun pass
   through the atmosphere and warm the Earth's surface.
2. The warm surface — like any warm surface — radiates energy back out
   as **[[infrared-radiation]]**.
3. Molecules such as CO₂ in the atmosphere **absorb** that infrared
   radiation.
4. The molecules then **re-emit the energy in all directions**,
   including back towards the ground — so the atmosphere, and the
   surface beneath it, end up warmer than they would otherwise be.

That is the greenhouse effect: not a glass roof, but infrared radiation
absorbed and re-emitted by molecules that the rest of the air ignores.
Scientists believe that the rising concentration of carbon dioxide is
intensifying this effect, and that the increase **may contribute to
climate change**. The exact pattern of change is difficult to predict,
but the effects scientists are most concerned about include: polar ice
caps melting, sea levels rising, and more extreme weather such as
floods, droughts and heatwaves.

:::did-you-know
Science is not a chorus, and this topic is a rare case where a
specification acknowledges the debate. Most scientists believe that
increases in carbon dioxide will cause devastating climate change. But
others reject this: they argue that the increases in average world
temperatures during the twentieth century were part of natural heating
and cooling cycles driven by the Sun and by changes in ocean currents,
and that the effect of carbon dioxide is small by comparison. The
scientific majority position is the one carried by the mark schemes —
but knowing the debate exists is part of knowing how evidence and
consensus work.
:::

:::did-you-know
Water vapour is a greenhouse gas too — an important one, as you will
see next section — but its concentration in the air swings between 0 and
4% with the weather. Carbon dioxide's share is far smaller and far
steadier, which is exactly what makes its *trend* so telling: a slow,
ratcheting rise with one chemical cause (combustion) and one biological
counterweight (photosynthesis) that deforestation weakens.
:::

:::cross-curricular
The greenhouse effect is where chemistry meets geography, economics and
politics head-on. The combustion equations in this section are the
chemical end of the energy debate: every energy choice a country makes
— coal, oil, gas, renewables, nuclear — is in part a decision about how
much CO₂ those equations release into the 0.04%. The consequences list
(melting ice caps, rising seas, extreme weather) is written in
geography; the response, in international treaties and carbon pricing,
is written in politics. Chemistry supplies the mechanism that all three
subjects argue about.
:::

:::exam-hint
Spec 2.13 says "know", but the know is precise: a greenhouse gas is one
that **absorbs infrared radiation** — the radiation emitted by the
Earth's surface — **and re-emits it in all directions**. Answers built
on "traps heat like the glass in a greenhouse" or "blocks the Sun's
rays" drop the mark, because both miss the actual mechanism: the Sun's
incoming light passes *through*, and it is the *outgoing infrared* that
the molecules catch. Name the radiation (infrared), name the source
(the Earth's surface), and name the re-emission (all directions).
:::

:::misconception
"The greenhouse effect is a bad thing we should eliminate." Read step
four again before agreeing. The greenhouse effect is what keeps the
Earth warm enough for water to be mostly liquid — without any
greenhouse gases the surface would be far too cold for life as we know
it. The problem is not the effect but its **enhancement**: extra carbon
dioxide from human activity strengthens an essential natural warming
into a destabilising one. Say "enhanced greenhouse effect" for the
problem and you have the concept exactly.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.13 items on carbon dioxide as a greenhouse
gas. Reconstruct the four-step mechanism in order; name the radiation
the Earth's surface emits; explain why burning coal adds CO₂ to the
atmosphere with an equation; and give two possible consequences of
climate change from the scientists' list.
:::

sections.title: Why Is Co2 a Greenhouse Gas and Oxygen and Nitrogen Are Not?
sections.markdown:
The presence of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere is essential to life
on Earth: they keep the planet at a temperature at which water is
mostly liquid. But it is just as important that the main constituents
of the air — nitrogen and oxygen — are *not* greenhouse gases. If they
were, the atmosphere would absorb outgoing infrared at every wavelength
and the Earth would be too hot to support life as we know it. So what
qualifies carbon dioxide and water vapour for a job that 99% of the air
cannot do?

The qualification rule first: a **[[greenhouse-gas]]** must be able to
**absorb infrared radiation** emitted by the Earth's surface and then
**emit it again in all directions**, warming the atmosphere. All
molecules vibrate — their bonds stretch and bend constantly. A molecule
can absorb infrared radiation when those vibrations involve a **change
in the polarity of the molecule**. Polarity is therefore the whole
story, and it is worth building the idea carefully.

**What is polarity?** A **[[polar-molecule]]** has one end slightly
negative and the other end slightly positive. Polarity arises because
different atoms attract the electrons in a covalent bond to different
extents — a property called **[[electronegativity]]** — and it also
depends on the shape of the molecule. Water is the classic example: the oxygen atom attracts the
shared electrons in both O–H bonds more strongly than the hydrogen
atoms do, so the oxygen end of the molecule carries a small negative
charge (δ−) and the hydrogen ends carry small positive charges (δ+).
The polarity of a water molecule changes as it vibrates, and that is
why **water vapour is an important greenhouse gas**.

Now apply the rule to the three gases that matter.

**Carbon dioxide** is a *non-polar* molecule as it stands: it is linear
— the three atoms sit in a straight line, O=C=O — and symmetrical, so
the bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. There is no
positive end and no negative end. But the molecule does not stand
still. As a CO₂ molecule **vibrates**, its geometry momentarily distorts
— the symmetric stretch and bend destroy the perfect symmetry for an
instant — and in those moments the molecule becomes non-symmetrical and
polar. Because its polarity **changes as it vibrates**, carbon dioxide
can absorb infrared radiation, and it is a greenhouse gas.

**Oxygen and nitrogen** are the opposite case in every particular. Each
molecule contains two *identical* atoms, so the electrons in the bond
are shared equally and there are no partial charges to begin with. When
the molecules vibrate, they have only one way of vibrating — the bond
simply stretches and compresses — and the molecule **remains
non-polar throughout**. No change in polarity means no ability to absorb
infrared radiation, so N₂ and O₂ are **not greenhouse gases**, whatever
their concentration.

That is the complete answer to the section's question, and it is a
genuine explanation — the kind that turns a "know" statement into
understanding. The atmosphere warms itself through the small fraction
of molecules whose vibrations keep changing their polarity, and the two
gases that dominate the air are transparent to infrared precisely
because identical atoms cannot build a dipole, vibrating or not.

:::summary
Dry air is approximately 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen, 0.9% argon and 0.04%
carbon dioxide (figures for dry, unpolluted air; water vapour adds up to
4% more). The percentage of oxygen can be measured by reacting a
reagent — heated copper, damp iron filings or burning phosphorus — with
the oxygen in a known volume of air and measuring the volume decrease:
copper gives 100 → 79 cm³ for 21%, iron gives the three-volume
calculation 234 → 185 cm³ for 49 cm³ used up ≈ 21%, and in every case
the reagent must be in **excess** so all the oxygen reacts; low results
come from too little time or too little reagent. Elements burn in
oxygen in **combustion** reactions: magnesium (bright white flame →
white MgO, slightly soluble to alkaline solution), sulfur (blue flame →
poisonous colourless SO₂, dissolving to **sulfurous** acid H₂SO₃) and
hydrogen (pale blue flame → water; H₂/O₂ mixtures explode — the squeaky
pop). Metal oxides are ionic and usually **basic**; non-metal oxides
are covalent and usually **acidic**. Carbon dioxide forms in the lab
from marble chips and dilute hydrochloric acid, and by **thermal
decomposition** of metal carbonates (green copper(II) carbonate → black
copper(II) oxide + CO₂; limestone → quicklime at high temperature). It
reaches the atmosphere from fossil-fuel combustion and it is a
**greenhouse gas**: it absorbs the infrared radiation the warm surface
emits and re-emits it in all directions, because its polarity changes
as it vibrates — while N₂ and O₂, with equally shared electrons and no
polarity change, absorb nothing.
:::

:::can-you
- state the four most abundant gases in dry air with their approximate
  percentages by volume (spec 2.9)?
- describe the copper, iron and phosphorus methods for determining the
  percentage of oxygen in air — and explain why the reagent must be in
  excess in each (spec 2.10, 2.14)?
- carry out the percentage calculation from raw volumes, including the
  three-volume iron apparatus (100 − 79 → 21%; 234 − 185 = 49, 49/234 ×
  100 ≈ 21%)?
- describe the combustion of magnesium, hydrogen and sulfur in oxygen
  with balanced equations and observations (spec 2.11)?
- write the equations for carbon dioxide from marble chips + HCl and
  from heating metal carbonates, with the copper(II) carbonate colour
  change (spec 2.12)?
- explain what a greenhouse gas is in terms of infrared absorption,
  re-emission and vibrating polarity — and why CO₂ qualifies while O₂
  and N₂ do not (spec 2.13)?
:::

:::exam-hint
The polarity explanation is a four-link chain, and mark schemes pay the
links separately: (1) all molecules vibrate; (2) a molecule absorbs IR
only if its vibration changes its polarity; (3) CO₂ is symmetric and
non-polar at rest, but vibration makes it momentarily polar — so it
absorbs; (4) O₂ and N₂ have two identical atoms, share electrons
equally and stay non-polar however they vibrate — so they cannot
absorb. Answers that just say "CO₂ absorbs IR but oxygen doesn't" earn
the first and last marks and lose the two reasoning links in between.
:::

:::misconception
"CO₂ is non-polar, so it cannot interact with infrared radiation at
all." Non-polar describes the molecule's *resting* shape — a straight,
symmetrical O=C=O line whose bond dipoles cancel. But the molecule is
vibrating, and the vibration repeatedly breaks the symmetry, creating a
momentary polarity that lets it absorb IR. The correct statement is
"non-polar at rest, polar in vibration" — the vibration *is* the
mechanism, not an obstacle to it.
:::

:::quick-check
Question-bank join: spec 2.13 items on the molecular explanation of the
greenhouse effect — the closing gate for the chapter's full 2.9–2.14
set. Deliver the four-link chain unprompted; explain why
water vapour is a greenhouse gas using the word electronegativity; and
say exactly why the two-identical-atoms structure of N₂ and O₂ disqualifies
them. If those three answers are fluent, this chapter is fully
assembled.
:::
